Primes from the Zeros

Game: Make waves add up to a staircase that climbs at every prime number.
How to play: Press "Add zeros" and watch the smooth green line learn where the primes are. Slide to add or remove zeros yourself.

Counting primes (ψ)Built from the zeros

Look for the math

This is why the zeros of the zeta function matter: each one is a wave, and together the waves spell out the primes. Riemann found this in 1859.

A staircase for the primes

Chebyshev's function ψ(x) adds ln p each time x passes a prime power p^k, so it is a staircase with steps at 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, … It is also ln lcm(1, 2, …, x); the test confirmed this up to 40. By the prime number theorem, ψ(x) is close to x.

Riemann's explicit formula

Riemann's explicit formula says ψ(x) = x − Σ x^ρ/ρ − ln 2π − ½ ln(1 − x⁻²), summed over the zeros ρ = ½ + iγ of the zeta function. A pair ½ ± iγ gives the real wave −2√x · (½ cos(γ ln x) + γ sin(γ ln x)) / (¼ + γ²). The test confirmed the real form against complex arithmetic, that the 100 zeros used here are zeros (the 29 below 100 matched the ones found on the previous page), and that the average error against the true staircase falls steadily as zeros are added: 0.92 with none, 0.53 with 10 and 0.16 with 100.

Where the hypothesis comes in

Each wave has size about √x / γ. If every zero has real part ½, as the Riemann Hypothesis says, no wave can outgrow √x, so ψ(x) stays within a square-root-sized distance of x. The test confirmed this: |ψ(x) − x| < √x ln²x / (8π) for every x from 74 to 20,000. A zero with real part above ½ would make a wave that grows faster than √x and eventually breaks this bound. Low zeros make big, slow waves; high zeros small, fast ones. You hear a drum from its overtones, and here you hear the primes from the zeros.

Tick "Flatten" and add zeros one by one. Which jumps does the first zero find? How does the picture sharpen when the 100th zero arrives?
